title: Melchizedek again (Hebrews 7)
hookLine: a priest without genealogy: Christ's priesthood forever
tomorrow: why would a teaching letter promise nobody will need teaching?

lines: BREAD AND WINE ON THE ROAD.
cards: Some people turn up in your life once, say the one thing you needed, and vanish. No last name, no follow-up. Genesis has a man like that.
Abraham is heading home from a battle, worn out, with the people he rescued.

And out of a city called Salem walks a king nobody has introduced: "And Melchizedek king of Salem brought forth bread and wine: and he was the priest of the most high God." He blesses Abraham. Abraham gives him a tenth.
Then the story moves on without him. Later a psalm names him once: "Thou art a priest for ever after the order of Melchizedek." So who was he?

teach.h: KING OF RIGHTEOUSNESS, KING OF PEACE.
teach.b: Hebrews seven takes the question on. First it translates the name itself: "first being by interpretation King of righteousness, and after that also King of Salem, which is, King of peace." Then it does something bolder.
It reads what Genesis leaves out. No parents. No birth, no death.

teach.h: NO FATHER, NO MOTHER, NO END.
teach.b: "Without father, without mother, without descent, having neither beginning of days, nor end of life; but made like unto the Son of God; abideth a priest continually."
Some readers take this as an argument from the story's silence; others read it more literally. Either way, here's why he matters to the writer: his story has no ending.
Other priests served, Hebrews says, until death stopped them, and others took their place.

teach.h: A PRIEST WHO NEVER HANDS OFF.

teach.b: And that is the line the whole chapter is building to: "Wherefore he is able also to save them to the uttermost that come unto God by him, seeing he ever liveth to make intercession for them."
Intercession is speaking to God on someone else's behalf. Ever liveth: still at it, this morning, tonight.

Here's the detail to tell a friend: the priest of Genesis meets Abraham carrying bread and wine, and some Christians hear an echo of the Lord's table in that. For Christians, the comfort in Hebrews seven is plain.
On the days a person can't find a single word, Hebrews says someone is still speaking for them.

how: Christians pray for one another by name, in church prayer lists and at home, and some also speak of Christ himself interceding for them, as Hebrews 7:25 says.

o: a prophet who wrote the letter to the Hebrews
an angel who stopped Abraham's sacrifice
a king-priest from Genesis whom Hebrews links to Jesus

games.q: the king from Salem — tap the pairs.
p: what he brought out to Abraham
speaking to God on someone's behalf

s: Melchizedek is a name Hebrews made up
he meets Abraham in Genesis 14, and a psalm names him too.
Genesis lists Melchizedek's parents and his death
it gives neither. Hebrews reads that silence: without father, without mother.
Hebrews translates his name as King of righteousness
and Salem, it says, means peace.

games.q: your church's prayer chain is collecting names. your friend says her grandpa would hate being on it: he's the one who prays for everybody else. what fits Hebrews 7?
o: leave him off; prayer is for people who can't pray.
add him only if he asks; it's his call alone.
the one who prays for others is prayed for too.
games.why: Hebrews says he ever liveth to make intercession for them: even the most faithful pray-er is held in someone else's prayer.

practice: Write one name on a scrap of paper: someone who can't pray for themselves right now, because they're sick, grieving or simply worn out. Hold the paper through the sit.
Those who pray can speak for that person now; anyone can keep the name in hand, on their behalf.

wordCard.voice: Melchizedek again. The king-priest of Salem from Genesis, read in Hebrews seven as a priest whose service has no end.

orig.note: Hebrew: the name in Genesis 14:18; Hebrews 7:2 renders it King of righteousness.

carryVoice: Your line: he always lives to pray. Ever liveth, Hebrews says, for them. See you tomorrow.
